plain: Ollama is a program that puts artificial intelligence inside your own computer. When you write to it, the answer doesn't travel to any company's servers: it gets computed right there, on your desk, with the computer you already have. It's the difference between ordering food delivery and having a kitchen at home: you pay nothing per dish, nobody sees what you're cooking, and it works even if the internet goes down, but you're limited to what fits in your kitchen. If your computer is modest, you'll have a modest cook, and it's best to accept that from minute one.

account.free: Completely free, no registration. No username, no password, no card, no daily message limit. You download the program, download the models, and that's it. The only thing you pay for is electricity and the disk space the models take up. There's a separate optional paid service, Ollama Cloud, for running huge models on someone else's servers when your machine isn't up to it: it ran around $20 a month, but the price has changed several times, so check ollama.com before trusting that figure. You don't need it for this course, and if you use it you lose exactly what makes Ollama special, which is that nothing leaves your computer.
steps: Go to ollama.com. The page is almost all white and has just one big black button in the center that says 'Download'. Don't confuse it with the 'Models' link at the top, which is just the catalog. Click 'Download'.

Three tabs appear: 'macOS', 'Windows', and 'Linux'. It usually picks yours automatically. Click the right one and a file between 200 and 700 MB (megabytes, about the size of a short movie) starts downloading. One or two minutes on fiber.

On Windows you download 'OllamaSetup.exe'. Double-click and a small window appears with an 'Install' button. It doesn't ask for administrator permissions or your computer's password: it installs inside your user folder. On Mac you download a .zip, open it, and drag the llama icon into the 'Applications' folder. The first time you open it, Mac will ask if you're sure you want to open an app downloaded from the internet: say yes.

Ollama doesn't open any big window once it finishes installing, and that throws people off. What you'll see is a small llama icon: on Windows, at the bottom right next to the clock, maybe hidden behind the '^' arrow that expands hidden icons; on Mac, at the top right in the menu bar. That icon means the engine is running in the background and waiting. If you don't see it, search for 'Ollama' in the start menu and open it.

Click the llama icon and a chat window opens, similar to any other. At the bottom, next to the box where you type, there's a dropdown with the model name. Choose a small one to start: 'llama3.2:3b' takes up about 2 GB and runs even on a laptop with 8 GB of memory. If you'd rather do it by typing commands, open the Terminal (on Windows search for 'Terminal' or 'PowerShell' in the start menu; on Mac it's in Applications, inside Utilities) and type: ollama run llama3.2:3b

The first time you'll see a progress bar with a percentage. It's about 2 GB, 2 to 10 minutes depending on your connection. This happens only once per model: after that it lives on your disk and starts in two seconds, with or without internet.

Type anything and press Enter. You'll see the words appearing one at a time, as if someone were typing on the other end. If you're in the Terminal, to exit the conversation type /bye, with the slash in front, and you're back at the normal command line. To see which models you have saved and how much space they take: ollama list. To delete one: ollama rm llama3.2:3b
account.warning: Every model you try stays on your hard drive forever until you delete it by hand. llama3.2:3b is 2 GB, llama3.1:8b about 4.7 GB, gemma3:27b about 17 GB. Three evenings of curiosity trying models and you've eaten up 30 or 40 GB without noticing, until your computer warns you it's out of space. Check what you have with 'ollama list' and delete what you don't use with 'ollama rm model-name'. That deletion is irreversible and doesn't go to the trash: if you regret it, you have to download the whole thing again. And a security warning: if a tutorial tells you to set OLLAMA_HOST to 0.0.0.0 to 'access it from your phone', don't do it while you're still learning. That opens your Ollama to the entire network you're on, and anyone connected to the same wifi (an office, a hotel, a café) can use your computer for whatever they want without you seeing it.

first: Open the chat window and type something short and silly, like 'explain what a mortgage is in three sentences'. Watch the speed at which the words come out: that's what your computer can deliver, and it's good to know that before getting your hopes up.
Cut the internet entirely: airplane mode, or turn off wifi. Ask it the same thing again. It answers the same way. That moment explains what Ollama is for better than any theory.

Check how much memory you really have before choosing anything else. On Windows, Ctrl+Shift+Esc opens Task Manager, 'Performance' tab, 'Memory' section. On Mac, Apple menu and 'About This Mac'. Write that number down: it controls everything else.
Type 'ollama list' in the Terminal and look at the size column. There you'll see exactly how many gigabytes your curiosity has cost. Get used to checking it every few days.

Give it a task it's good at and one it's not. Hand it a convoluted email and ask it to rewrite it in three lines: it'll do fine. Then ask it what the interest rate closed at last month: it'll make it up. With those two examples you'll know what to trust it with.
shortcuts: ollama run model-name
The command that does it all: if the model isn't there, it downloads it; if it is, it loads it and opens the conversation. It's 80% of your daily use. Example: ollama run llama3.1:8b
/bye

Typed inside the conversation, with the slash in front, and it returns you to the normal Terminal line. The model stays in memory for about 5 minutes in case you come back. On Mac and Linux, Ctrl+D does the same.
Ctrl+C

Cuts off a response halfway without closing anything. You'll use it every day: as soon as you see the model has misunderstood the question, cut it off and rephrase instead of waiting through three useless paragraphs.
ollama list
The list of everything you have downloaded, with its size in gigabytes and when you downloaded it. It's your hard drive's receipt. Check it before downloading anything new.
ollama ps
Shows which model is loaded in memory right now and how much space it takes. When your computer starts acting weird, this command tells you in two seconds whether it's Ollama's fault.
ollama stop model-name
Unloads the model from memory instantly, without waiting the usual 5 minutes. It's the 'give me back my RAM' button when you're about to open Photoshop or a video call.
/set parameter num_ctx 8192

Inside the conversation, expands the model's field of view before you paste a long document. It defaults to short and cuts things off from behind without warning. It costs memory, so only raise it when you need it.
/set verbose

Inside the conversation, makes it show you, after every response, the real speed in word-chunks per second. It's the only honest way to compare two models on YOUR computer, instead of trusting internet tables.
/clear

Clears the current conversation's memory without exiting or reloading the model. Use it when switching topics: otherwise the model keeps dragging along the previous subject and it contaminates the answers.
Up arrow
In the Terminal, brings back the last command you typed. Saves you from retyping 'ollama run qwen2.5-coder:7b' forty times a day.
daily: One single model, one that fits comfortably, for 90% of the work. With 16 GB of memory that's llama3.1:8b or qwen2.5:7b. Switching models every couple of days is the best way to learn nothing: stick with one until you know exactly where it fails.

Rewriting, translating, shortening, and changing the tone of text YOU already have in front of you. It's what a small model does best, because it doesn't need to know anything about the world: just transform what you give it. Emails, product descriptions, review replies, legal text in plain language.

Repetitive, high-volume work: sorting 800 emails by topic, pulling the ID and amount from 300 invoices in text, tagging comments as positive or negative. This is where local wins decisively over the cloud, because the cost per item is zero and you can leave it running all night.

Expanding the context before pasting something long. Enter with 'ollama run your-model', type '/set parameter num_ctx 8192', and then paste the document. If you don't, the model only keeps the end of the text and answers as confidently as if it had read the whole thing.

Watching memory with 'ollama ps' and releasing it with 'ollama stop'. An 8B model keeps occupying almost 5 GB for 5 minutes after you finish. If your computer drags right when you close the conversation, this is why.

Disk cleanup once a month: 'ollama list', check what you haven't touched, and 'ollama rm name'. It's irreversible and doesn't go to the trash, but redownloading it takes ten minutes. Better that than running out of space on your system drive.

Split the work honestly: the confidential stuff, the repetitive stuff, and whatever has to work without internet, here; the hard stuff, the long stuff, and whatever can't afford to be wrong, on a paid cloud model. It's not a competition, they're two different tools.

templates.name: Decision table: which model based on your computer
templates.what: The answer to the only question that matters on day one. Good for anyone who doesn't know whether their machine can handle it and doesn't want to download 20 GB just to find out it can't. It's a napkin calculation: total memory minus 4 GB that Windows or macOS plus the browser keep for themselves, and what's left is your real ceiling.
templates.how: 1) Check your memory: Windows, Ctrl+Shift+Esc, 'Performance' tab, 'Memory'. Mac, Apple menu and 'About This Mac'. 2) Find your range below. 3) Copy the line starting with 'ollama pull' and paste it into the Terminal. 4) Once it's done, run it with 'ollama run' and the same name. Sizes are approximate and change with versions: check yours with 'ollama list' after downloading.
fill: Your RAM in gigabytes
The number shown in Task Manager or 'About This Mac'
Whether you have an NVIDIA graphics card and how many gigabytes
Task Manager, 'Performance', 'GPU'; look for 'Dedicated GPU memory'
What you want it for
General text, code, or reading images and scanned documents
templates.code:
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# FIRST: check your memory
#   Windows -> Ctrl+Shift+Esc -> Performance tab -> Memory
#   Mac     -> Apple menu -> About This Mac
# Rule: total memory - 4 GB (system and browser) = your real ceiling
# ---------------------------------------------------------------

# 8 GB RAM  (basic office laptop, usable ceiling ~4 GB)
ollama pull llama3.2:3b          # ~2 GB    general use, runs easily
ollama pull gemma3:4b            # ~3.3 GB  a bit better, tight fit
# With 8 GB don't try anything 7B or above. It won't fit.

# 16 GB RAM  (typical work laptop, usable ceiling ~12 GB)
ollama pull llama3.1:8b          # ~4.7 GB  the all-rounder
ollama pull qwen2.5:7b           # ~4.7 GB  very good in Spanish/other languages
ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:7b     # ~4.7 GB  for code
ollama pull phi4                 # 14B, ~9 GB  better, but close Chrome

# 32 GB RAM (or 32 GB Mac, usable ceiling ~26 GB)
ollama pull gemma3:27b           # ~17 GB
ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:32b    # ~20 GB  for code, very solid
ollama pull gpt-oss:20b          # ~14 GB

# 64 GB or more (or Mac Studio / expensive desktop rig)
ollama pull llama3.3:70b         # ~43 GB

# EXTRA: reading images and screenshots (needs ~2 GB more than its size)
ollama pull llama3.2-vision      # 11B, ~7.9 GB   needs 16 GB or more
ollama pull gemma3:4b            # ~3.3 GB        also reads images

# EXTRA: searching inside your own documents (indexing model)
ollama pull nomic-embed-text     # ~274 MB, fits on anything

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# DAILY MAINTENANCE
ollama list                      # what I have and how much it takes up
ollama ps                        # what's loaded in memory RIGHT NOW
ollama stop llama3.1:8b          # release the memory instantly
ollama rm gemma3:27b             # delete from disk (IRREVERSIBLE)
ollama show llama3.1:8b          # model card: context, license
# ---------------------------------------------------------------

templates.name: Modelfile: your company assistant, with the rules baked in
templates.what: A model of your own, with its own name, that already knows who you are, how you write, and what it shouldn't do, without you having to repeat it every conversation. Good for anyone who runs the same kind of task every day: customer service, product descriptions, review replies, internal notes.
templates.how: 1) Create a folder on the Desktop, for example 'my-assistant'. 2) Inside it, create a text file and name it Modelfile, with NO extension. Watch out with Windows Notepad: when saving, under 'Save as type' choose 'All Files' and type the name in quotes, "Modelfile", or you'll end up with a Modelfile.txt that doesn't work. 3) Paste the code below inside and change what's in brackets. 4) Open the Terminal, go to that folder with 'cd Desktop\my-assistant' and type: ollama create assistant -f Modelfile. Takes a few seconds and doesn't download anything new if you already have the base model. 5) Use it with: ollama run assistant. 6) If you regret it: ollama rm assistant. It only deletes your version, the base model stays.
fill: FROM llama3.1:8b
The base model that fits according to the table above. With 8 GB of RAM use llama3.2:3b
[YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
The name of your company or project
[TYPE OF BUSINESS] in [CITY]
What you do and where. Example: dental clinic in Austin
[HOURS] and [EMAIL]
The details you repeat a hundred times a day in emails
num_ctx 8192
Raise it to 16384 if you're going to paste long documents and have 32 GB. Lower it to 4096 if you have 8 GB
temperature 0.4
The lower, the more literal and repetitive; the higher, the more creative and inventive. For serious work, between 0.2 and 0.5
templates.code:
FROM llama3.1:8b

PARAMETER num_ctx 8192
PARAMETER temperature 0.4
PARAMETER top_p 0.9

SYSTEM """
You are the internal assistant for [YOUR BUSINESS NAME], a [TYPE OF BUSINESS] in [CITY].

HOW YOU WRITE
- Always in professional English.
- Short sentences. No intros like "sure, here you go".
- No closing summaries or "hope this helps".
- Never use emojis.

WHAT YOU DON'T DO
- If you don't know something, write exactly: I DON'T KNOW. And stop there.
- Never make up prices, dates, deadlines, people's names, legal citations,
  or case numbers. Not even as an example.
- Never promise anything on the company's behalf: discounts, delivery
  times, or refunds unless I've given them to you in the message.

FIXED DATA YOU CAN USE
- Hours: [HOURS]
- Contact email: [EMAIL]
- Return policy: [SUMMARIZE IT IN ONE SENTENCE]

OUTPUT FORMAT
- When asked for customer-facing text, return it ready to copy and
  paste, with no comments around it and no explaining what you did.
- When asked for a list, return only the list.
"""

templates.name: Processing a whole folder of files, one by one, without touching anything
templates.what: A small script that grabs every .txt file in a folder, feeds it to your local model with the same instruction, and drops each result in another folder. This is the case where having AI at home clearly wins: 500 files through the cloud is dozens of dollars, here it's zero dollars and one night with the computer left on.
templates.how: 1) Copy the code into Notepad and save it on the Desktop as process.ps1 (under 'Save as type' choose 'All Files' and type the name in quotes). 2) Change the first five lines: the two folders, the model, and the instruction. 3) Right-click on the file, 'Run with PowerShell'. 4) If Windows tells you script execution is disabled, open PowerShell and type: powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File "$HOME\Desktop\process.ps1". 5) You'll see one line per file with a counter. Let it run. This is Windows-only; if you're on Mac, ask the AI to translate it into a shell script and tell it the commands are the same.
fill: $inputFolder
The path to the folder where your .txt files are. Copy it from Explorer's address bar
$outputFolder
Where you want the results. If it doesn't exist, it gets created automatically
$model
The exact name shown in 'ollama list'
$instruction
What you're asking of each file. Be brutally specific and tell it the exact format of the response
templates.code:
# SAVE THIS AS: process.ps1  (Windows only)
# WHAT IT DOES: takes every .txt file in a folder, feeds it to your local
# model with the same instruction, and saves each response in another folder.
# It does NOT delete or modify your original files.

$inputFolder  = "$HOME\Desktop\inputs"
$outputFolder = "$HOME\Desktop\results"
$model        = "llama3.1:8b"
$instruction  = "Summarize this text in 3 sentences. Then write one last line starting with ACTION: followed by what needs to be done. If there's nothing to do, write ACTION: none."

New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path $outputFolder | Out-Null

$files = Get-ChildItem -Path $inputFolder -Filter *.txt
$total = $files.Count
$n = 0

if ($total -eq 0) {
    Write-Host "No .txt files found in $inputFolder. Check the path."
    return
}

Write-Host "About to process $total files with $model. This may take a while."

foreach ($file in $files) {
    $n++
    Write-Host "[$n/$total] $($file.Name)"
    $text = Get-Content -Path $file.FullName -Raw -Encoding UTF8

    $body = @{
        model  = $model
        prompt = "$instruction`n`n--- TEXT ---`n`n$text"
        stream = $false
    } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 3

    try {
        $bytes = [System.Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetBytes($body)
        $response = Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "http://localhost:11434/api/generate" -Method Post -Body $bytes -ContentType "application/json"
        $destination = Join-Path $outputFolder ($file.BaseName + "-result.txt")
        $response.response | Out-File -FilePath $destination -Encoding utf8
    } catch {
        Write-Host "  FAILED on $($file.Name): $($_.Exception.Message)"
    }
}

Write-Host ""
Write-Host "Done. Results are in: $outputFolder"

templates.name: Plugging your local model into your code editor (Continue in VS Code)
templates.what: Making the assistant that writes code for you inside the editor the one on your own computer instead of a paid one. Good for vibecoding without spending a dollar, for working on a train with no signal, and for client projects whose code can't leave your machine.
templates.how: 1) In VS Code, click the little squares icon in the left sidebar (Extensions), search for 'Continue', and click 'Install'. 2) Download the models: ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:7b and ollama pull nomic-embed-text. 3) Open Continue's configuration file: it's at C:\Users\YOUR_USER\.continue\config.yaml on Windows, or ~/.continue/config.yaml on Mac. If the .continue folder doesn't show up in Explorer, it's because it's hidden: type %USERPROFILE%\.continue in the address bar and press Enter. 4) Paste the content below. 5) Save and restart VS Code. Note: Continue has changed its configuration format between versions; older ones used config.json. If you open the folder and see a config.json instead of a config.yaml, hand this text to the AI and ask it to convert it to Continue's JSON format.
fill: model: qwen2.5-coder:7b
The code model that fits your machine. With 8 GB of RAM, qwen2.5-coder:1.5b. With 32 GB, qwen2.5-coder:32b
provider: ollama
Don't touch it. It's what tells Continue to look on your computer instead of the internet
apiBase
Only if you've changed the port. By default it's http://localhost:11434 and you don't need to set it
templates.code:
name: My local configuration
version: 1.0.0
schema: v1

models:
  - name: Local chat
    provider: ollama
    model: qwen2.5-coder:7b
    roles:
      - chat
      - edit
      - apply
    defaultCompletionOptions:
      contextLength: 8192

  - name: Local autocomplete
    provider: ollama
    model: qwen2.5-coder:1.5b-base
    roles:
      - autocomplete

  - name: My file search
    provider: ollama
    model: nomic-embed-text
    roles:
      - embed

context:
  - provider: file
  - provider: code
  - provider: diff
  - provider: terminal

errors: Error: model requires more system memory (5.6 GiB) than is available (3.2 GiB)

The clearest one of all: the model doesn't fit in memory. It's not the disk, it's the RAM, and there's no trick around it. Close Chrome, Teams, and whatever else you have open and try again; if it's still the same, drop down a size tier (from 14B to 8B, from 8B to 3B). Check with 'ollama ps' that no other model is loaded eating up memory, and unload it with 'ollama stop name'.
Error: llama runner process has terminated: signal: killed  (or on Windows: exit status 0xc0000409)

The engine died mid-response. Nine times out of ten it's memory again, but further down the line: not while loading, but while generating, usually because you raised num_ctx or pasted a huge chunk of text. Lower the context with '/set parameter num_ctx 4096', split the document into pieces, or use a smaller model. If it always happens with the same model, delete it with 'ollama rm' and redownload it: it may have gotten corrupted.
Error: could not connect to ollama app, is it running?

The engine is off. You're typing commands and nobody's on the other end. Check whether the llama icon is next to the clock (Windows, maybe behind the '^' arrow) or in the menu bar (Mac). If it's not there, search for 'Ollama' in the start menu and open it. Happens a lot after restarting the computer if you disabled it from starting automatically.
ollama : The term 'ollama' is not recognized as the name of a cmdlet, function, script file, or operable program.

The program is installed, but the Terminal window you had open doesn't know it, because it was opened before installation. Close it completely and open a new one. If it's still the same after that, restart the computer. Only if it persists is it a real installation problem: uninstall and reinstall from ollama.com.
Error: pull model manifest: file does not exist

You got the name or the tag wrong. Names are literal and case-sensitive down to the letter: 'llama3.2:3b' exists, 'llama3.2:3B' or 'llama-3.2:3b' don't. Go to ollama.com, click 'Models', find the model, and copy the exact command shown on the right, tag included. Also watch out for size tags: not every model has a 3b version.

The download got cut off halfway. Usually weak wifi or an overloaded server. Run the same 'ollama pull' again: it doesn't start from zero, it resumes where it left off, because it downloads in chunks. If it cuts off three times in a row, switch to a cable or try at a different time. It's not your computer's fault.
Error: listen tcp 127.0.0.1:11434: bind: Only one usage of each socket address (protocol/network address) is normally permitted.

You typed 'ollama serve' when Ollama was already running. It's a clash with itself, not a real failure. On Windows and Mac you never need to type 'ollama serve': the program starts on its own with the system. Close that window and use 'ollama run' directly.
The model answers a word every several seconds and the fan is roaring (with no error message at all)

The most deceptive symptom, because there's no error: the model almost fits, and the computer is going back and forth to the disk for every word-chunk. The disk is about a hundred times slower than memory, so you don't go from 20 words a second to 10, you go to one every three seconds. Type '/set verbose' to see the real number, and if it's below 5 chunks per second, switch to a smaller model. What you need isn't patience, it's a different model.

prompts.name: Have the AI pick the exact model for your computer
prompts.prompt: Act as a technician who sets up local AI models with Ollama and is talking to someone who has never coded. Here are my specs: operating system [WINDOWS 11 / MACOS / LINUX], total RAM [16] GB, graphics card [NONE DEDICATED / NVIDIA RTX 4060 8 GB / APPLE M2 CHIP], free disk space [120] GB, and processor [INTEL I5 / RYZEN 7 / APPLE M2]. What I mainly want to do with the model is [SUMMARIZE CONTRACTS AND REWRITE EMAILS], and secondarily [GENERATE CODE FOR A SIMPLE WEBSITE]. The documents I'll feed it average [4] pages. Give me the following and nothing else: first, a recommended main model with its exact 'ollama pull' command and its size in gigabytes; second, a smaller backup plan in case the main one is slow, with its command; third, the explicit calculation of how much free memory I'll have left while the model is running, accounting for the system and browser eating about 4 GB; fourth, how many word-chunks per second I can realistically expect from this machine, and whether that's comfortable to read or maddening; fifth, three specific tasks from my list this model will handle well and three it'll handle badly, with the reason in one sentence each. If my machine can't handle what I want, tell me straight out in the first line instead of recommending something that won't work for me. Don't explain what Ollama is, I already have it installed.

prompts.name: Diagnose why it's slow or why it's giving an error
prompts.prompt: I have Ollama installed on my computer and something's wrong. I don't know how to code, so I need instructions I can copy and paste exactly as they are, without having to interpret anything. My machine has [16] GB of RAM, [NO DEDICATED GRAPHICS CARD / AN NVIDIA WITH 8 GB], system [WINDOWS 11]. The model I'm using is [LLAMA3.1:8B]. What I was doing when it failed: [PASTING A 30-PAGE DOCUMENT AND ASKING FOR A SUMMARY]. The literal error message, copied exactly as it shows on screen, is: [PASTE THE FULL ERROR HERE]. If there's no error message, the symptom is: [IT TAKES ALMOST A MINUTE TO START RESPONDING AND THE FAN GOES CRAZY]. I want you to do four things. One: translate that error into plain English, in two sentences, telling me whether the problem is memory, disk, network, a misspelled name, or the program not being started. Two: give me the exact commands to check my diagnosis, one per line, and tell me what specific numbers to look at in each one's response and what figure would be worrying. Three: give me the most likely fix, with the complete commands in order, explicitly warning me if any of them deletes something irreversibly. Four: tell me what I should do differently next time so this doesn't happen again. Order it from most likely to least likely and don't give me five parallel hypotheses: start with the one you'd bet money on.

prompts.name: Build your own model with fixed rules (Modelfile)
prompts.prompt: I want to create a custom model in Ollama, with my rules baked in, so I don't have to repeat them every conversation. I need the complete Modelfile, ready to copy and paste, plus the exact commands to create and test it. I don't know how to code: don't give me loose fragments or tell me 'add your configuration here'. My business is [AN ONLINE SHOP FOR HANDMADE GOODS] in [AUSTIN]. I'm going to use the assistant to [ANSWER CUSTOMER EMAILS AND WRITE PRODUCT DESCRIPTIONS]. My base model is [LLAMA3.1:8B] and I have [16] GB of RAM. I want it to always write in professional English, short sentences, no emojis, and never make up prices, delivery times, or return policies: if it doesn't know, it has to say I DON'T KNOW and stop. The fixed data it can use is: hours [9 TO 6, MONDAY THROUGH FRIDAY], email [HELLO@MYSHOP.COM], and returns [30 DAYS, NO QUESTIONS ASKED]. Give me: the whole Modelfile with the SYSTEM block written in English and thoroughly detailed; the num_ctx and temperature values that suit my memory and type of work, explaining each in one sentence; the command to create it; the command to use it; the command to delete it if I regret it, warning me whether that also deletes the base model; and three example sentences to test that the rules actually stuck, including one trap to check whether it makes up a fact.

prompts.name: Set up batch processing of your files, locally and for free
prompts.prompt: I want to use my local Ollama model to process a lot of files at once, without going through them one by one by hand. I don't know how to code: give me the whole script, commented in English, and instructions on how to save and run it with real menu and button names. I'm on [WINDOWS 11], my model is [LLAMA3.1:8B], and I have [16] GB of RAM. The files are [340 .TXT FILES WITH CALL TRANSCRIPTS], they're in the folder [C:\USERS\NAME\DESKTOP\CALLS], and average [8] KB each. From each file I want to pull [THE CUSTOMER'S NAME, THE REASON FOR THE CALL, AND WHETHER IT WAS RESOLVED OR NOT], and I want the result in [A SINGLE CSV FILE I CAN OPEN WITH EXCEL]. I need the script to: never touch or delete the original files; show an on-screen counter like 12 of 340 so I know where it's at; not stop entirely if one file fails, but note it and continue; and correctly preserve accented letters and special characters, which is where these things usually break. Also tell me roughly how long it'll take with my machine, whether I can leave it running overnight, whether the computer will be unusable in the meantime, and how to stop it partway through without messing things up. Before the script, write me the exact instruction to give the model so it always returns the same format and doesn't start explaining things on its own.

prompts.name: Decide whether a specific task belongs on your computer or in the cloud
prompts.prompt: Help me decide, for a specific task, whether I should use a model on my own computer with Ollama or pay for a cloud model. I don't want a speech about the pros and cons of each: I want a recommendation with a reason. The task is: [CLASSIFYING CUSTOMER SERVICE EMAILS BY ISSUE TYPE]. The volume is [ABOUT 900 ITEMS A MONTH] and each item is about [300] words. The data includes [NAMES, EMAILS, AND ORDER NUMBERS OF REAL CUSTOMERS], and over that I have authority, or [MY CLIENT / THE LEGAL DEPARTMENT] does. If it gets it wrong occasionally, [IT COSTS ME ONE MISCLASSIFIED EMAIL AND LITTLE ELSE / IT COSTS ME A CUSTOMER]. My computer has [16] GB of RAM. Analyze this and answer me in this order: first, your recommendation in a single sentence, local or cloud, no hedging; second, the estimated monthly cost in dollars of doing it in the cloud at that volume, saying what price per million word-chunks you're assuming and warning me that prices change and I should check them; third, what it would cost me locally, counting electricity and hours of computer time tied up; fourth, how much weight data-privacy regulations carry here if that information leaves my company; fifth, whether a hybrid solution makes sense, with the local model doing a first pass and the paid one handling only doubtful cases, and how you'd decide which cases are doubtful. Finish by telling me what specific signal I should watch for to know I chose the wrong option.

words: Model

The file containing everything the machine learned by reading text. It's what actually does the thinking. Weighs between 1 and 40 gigabytes and downloads once. Ollama is just the program that opens it and makes it talk, like the player that opens a movie: the player is small, the movie is heavy.
Parameters (the B in 3B, 8B, 70B)

The number of internal dials in the model, measured in billions. 8B means eight billion dials. More dials, better answers, and more memory used. Rule of thumb: a model takes up a bit more than half its number in gigabytes. 3B weighs about 2 GB, 8B about 4.7 GB, 14B about 9 GB, 27B about 17 GB, 70B about 43 GB.
Quantization

Saving the model with less precision so it takes up less space and runs faster, accepting a small loss of quality. Like moving a good camera's photo to your phone: looks nearly the same and takes up four times less space. Ollama already delivers it compressed by default, and that's the right choice 95% of the time, so you don't have to choose anything.
RAM

The computer's work desk. The whole model has to fit on top of that desk while it's working; having it in the drawer, which is the hard drive, isn't enough. If it doesn't fit, the computer starts going back and forth to the drawer for every word and everything becomes unbearable. It's the number that decides which models you can actually use.
VRAM

The graphics card's own memory, the part that draws video games. It's a separate desk, much faster for this. If you have a dedicated graphics card (NVIDIA cards with 'RTX' in the name), its memory is what matters, not the computer's: with 8 GB on the card, an 8B model flies; if it doesn't fit, the work gets split and speed drops sharply. On modern Macs there aren't two desks but one shared one, which is why they perform surprisingly well.
Context window (num_ctx)

How much text it can hold in front of it at once, counting what you write and what it has already answered. It's its field of view, not its long-term memory: whatever falls off the edge stops existing for it. In Ollama it comes short by default, around 4,000 word-chunks depending on the version, which is about 3,000 words, six or seven pages. It's expanded with /set parameter num_ctx 8192, and each expansion eats more memory.
Tokens per second

The speed at which it writes, measured in word-chunks per second. As a guide: 20 is a comfortable read, similar to someone typing fast; 5 is slower than you read and already gets tiring; 1 isn't usable for work. An 8B model runs around 20 on a recent Mac, 40 or 50 with a decent NVIDIA card, and around 5 on a normal office laptop with no graphics card.
Modelfile

A four-line recipe that creates a model of your own from another one: you take an existing one, add some fixed instructions, and give it a name. It doesn't train anything or download anything new, it just pins a permanent note to its forehead. It's the difference between explaining who you are every morning and having it already know.
Local server (localhost:11434)

The little door Ollama leaves open inside your own computer so other programs can talk to it: your code editor, a spreadsheet, a script. That number, 11434, is the internal address. It's not open to the internet, only to what's running on your machine, and that's why it's safe as long as you don't change it by hand.
Terminal

The window, black or white, where you type commands instead of clicking buttons. On Windows you open it by searching 'Terminal' in the start menu; on Mac it's in Applications, inside Utilities. It's intimidating the first time and nothing bad happens if you type something wrong: if you make a mistake, it just says it doesn't understand and that's the end of it. Ollama can be used without touching it, but it's more convenient with it.
matters: Memory rules everything, and the calculation is a napkin one: total memory minus 4 GB kept by the system and browser, and what's left is your ceiling. With 8 GB you're working with 3B or 4B models (llama3.2:3b, gemma3:4b) and not much more. With 16 GB, which is typical for a work laptop, your sweet spot is a 7B or 8B (llama3.1:8b, qwen2.5:7b, about 4.7 GB), and you can reach 14B (phi4, about 9 GB) if you close Chrome. With 32 GB, gemma3:27b, 17 GB, fits. 70B models need 48 GB or more, and that's already an expensive machine. Ignoring this hurts because the computer doesn't tell you clearly: it just starts taking a minute per response and you conclude Ollama is junk, when what happened is you picked a model that doesn't fit.

The context window comes short by default and doesn't warn you when you exceed it. You paste a 40-page report, the model only keeps the end, and it answers with total confidence as if it had read the whole thing. There's no error message, no red warning: just an answer that looks good and has made up half its premise. If you're going to work with long documents, expand it by typing '/set parameter num_ctx 8192' inside the conversation, knowing each expansion eats more memory. And if the document is huge, split it yourself first.

An 8B model on your laptop is not ChatGPT or Claude, and confusing them is the most expensive mistake you can make. The big companies' models have hundreds of billions of internal dials and run in rooms full of machines. Yours fits in 5 GB. That means: it chokes on long reasoning, gets lost in code that touches several files, mixes up dates, and makes up citations, court rulings, and legal statutes with total confidence. It's good for rephrasing, translating, summarizing something you've already read, classifying hundreds of emails, pulling loose facts out of a text, and producing a rough first draft. It's bad for anything where a false answer costs you money, a customer, or someone's wellbeing.

The point of having it at home is confidentiality and volume, not quality. If you handle payroll, medical records, unsigned contracts, or customer data, a local model is the only honest way to use AI without that information leaving your building, and with data protection regulations looming that's worth a lot. Same with volume: processing 20,000 records through the cloud is tens or hundreds of dollars in billing, and locally it's one night with the computer on and zero dollars. But if your task isn't confidential, isn't massive, and doesn't need to work offline, you're probably better off paying for a cloud model and keeping the quality.
ignore: The compression acronyms: Q4_K_M, Q5_0, Q8, GGUF, llama.cpp. It's a whole world with forums and arguments. Ollama picks a very sensible option for you when you just type the model name, and that option is the right one for almost everything. Come back here the day you have memory to spare and want to squeeze out the last 3% of quality.

The ranking tables and internet comparisons: MMLU, HumanEval, who overtook whom this week. They're measured on machines that aren't yours, with tasks that aren't yours. The only test that's worth anything is taking your ten real tasks, giving them to two models on your computer, and seeing which one serves you. Type '/set verbose' and you'll also get the real speed, which is a number no table will ever give you.

Ollama Cloud, giant 70B or 120B models, and fine-tuning a model with your own data. The first two need hardware or money you don't need right now; the third is a whole project in itself, and in 95% of cases a good SYSTEM block in a Modelfile gets you the same result in five minutes for free.

questions.prompt: You have a work laptop with 16 GB of memory and no dedicated graphics card. You want to summarize contracts, and a forum tells you 'the really good one' is llama3.3:70b, which takes up about 43 GB. You have plenty of disk space. What's going to happen if you install it?

options.text: It won't fit: with 16 GB your real ceiling is an 8B model (about 4.7 GB), or at most a 14B one (about 9 GB) with everything else closed. The sensible choice is llama3.1:8b or qwen2.5:7b.
options.why: Correct, and the nuance that makes it correct is that the limit isn't set by the disk but by memory: the model has to fit entirely on the work desk while it's answering, having it stored isn't enough. Subtracting the 4 GB the system and browser take, you have about 12 GB usable, and 43 doesn't fit into 12 no matter what. One more detail: on a laptop with no graphics card, even that 8B will run at about 5 words a second. Use it knowing that.

options.text: It'll work just as well, only slower. It's a matter of being patient and letting it work while you grab a coffee.
options.why: It's really believed because that's how almost all software behaves: a heavy program runs slow, but it runs. Here it breaks on the scale. When the model doesn't fit, the computer goes fetching pieces from the disk for every word-chunk it generates, and the disk is about a hundred times slower than memory. You don't go from 20 words a second to 10: you go to one word every several seconds, fan at full blast. And often it doesn't even start: it errors out with insufficient memory and closes.

options.text: If the hard drive has room, it doesn't matter: the model gets read from disk as needed, that's what the disk is for.
options.why: It's a reasonable intuition because that's how a video or a video game works, loading in pieces as you go. But a model isn't read in ordered chunks: to produce each word-chunk it needs to consult virtually all of its internal dials at once. That's why it has to be entirely in fast memory. The disk is only for storing it between sessions, never for working from it.

questions.explain: The disk decides how many models you can store; memory decides which ones you can actually use.

questions.prompt: You're on a train with no signal and you ask gemma3:4b, running on your laptop, about a recent Supreme Court ruling on layoffs. It answers with a case number, a date, a court, and a two-paragraph summary that sounds flawless. What do you do with that answer?

options.text: You don't trust any of it: not the number, not the date, not the content. You keep it as a draft outline and verify it against a real source as soon as you have signal.
options.why: Correct, and the nuance is that the problem isn't just that it has no internet, though that's part of it: it's that a 4B model fills gaps with what statistically looks like a ruling, and a made-up citation looks exactly like a real one. It doesn't even know that it doesn't know, so you won't see any hesitation in its tone. The only usable part there is the shape of the text, never the facts.

options.text: Since it's local, it hasn't gone through any server and nobody could have tampered with the answer: it's more reliable than asking a cloud tool.
options.why: Sounds logical and mixes up two unrelated things. Your data not leaving your computer is a privacy advantage, real and important. Accuracy is a different axis entirely: it depends on the model's size and whether it can consult sources. On that axis, four billion internal dials with no internet access is about as unreliable as it gets. Private and correct aren't the same thing.

options.text: You ask it to cite the exact source. If it can give you the specific reference, that means the answer was good.
options.why: It's the natural reaction, which is exactly why it's so deceptive. The flaw is that asking for the source doesn't trigger any verification: the model generates the citation with the same mechanism it used to generate the answer. It'll hand you back a perfectly formatted case number, a plausible official record, and a believable date, all made up. Asking a model with no search access for its source doesn't reduce the fabrication, it just disguises it better.

questions.explain: Going local gets you privacy and zero cost, not truth: for verifiable facts you need something that can actually look outside.
